profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting between a faculty lead and a research engineer/postdoc in an NLP meta-research lab who are planning a follow-up project inspired by a recent paper on causal influences in computational linguistics publication behavior. The context is that they want to turn the prior case-study findings into a sharper, publishable study on how methods, tasks, funding signals, and researcher location shape adoption and retirement patterns in the CL community. The agenda is to generate promising study angles, identify a feasible pilot, and agree on what existing data/pipelines they can reuse without yet locking in a full design. The expected outcome is a shortlist of 2-3 candidate project directions and a loosely shared plan for a pilot analysis using ACL Anthology-derived metadata and text features.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Causal inference, computational social science, NLP meta-research
members.background: Maya leads a small lab studying the evolution of machine learning fields and previously published a mixed-method paper on causal influences in computational linguistics publication trends.
members.private_state: She wants a follow-up project that can support a strong causal narrative for a high-prestige interdisciplinary venue, and she is wary of analyses that become descriptively rich but methodologically hard to defend.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'ACL Anthology' in project planning, they usually mean archival flagship conference papers and journals rather than the entire long tail of workshops, demos, and Findings volumes.

An 'adoption' of a method is most meaningful at the community-year level, such as when a technique becomes a visible share of published papers rather than when an individual author first experiments with it.

A 'robustness pass' for this kind of project primarily means causal-identification stress tests like placebo timing, alternative lag structures, and sensitivity analyses, not pipeline engineering checks.
The earlier 'China effect' result refers to the published analysis based on author location at publication and its association with work on non-English languages.

members.name: Leo Martínez
members.role: Senior Research Engineer and postdoctoral collaborator
members.expertise: Scholarly data pipelines, information extraction, bibliometrics, NLP systems
members.background: Leo maintains the lab's ACL Anthology ingestion pipeline, has built author-affiliation disambiguation tools, and often translates broad research questions into scalable data products.
members.private_state: He wants the project to leverage existing infrastructure and yield a reusable benchmark-grade dataset, and he prefers ideas that are operationally rich even if the causal framing stays somewhat broad.
hidden_assumptions: When collaborators say 'ACL Anthology,' they usually mean the full indexed ecosystem, including workshops, Findings, demos, and short papers, because that is the natural unit in the ingestion pipeline.
An 'adoption' event is best defined at the author or lab level as the first time a researcher uses a method, followed by repeat use as persistence.
A 'robustness pass' normally means checking that results survive extraction choices such as lexicon versions, affiliation matching, and venue-inclusion filters.
The earlier 'China effect' is the internal exploratory pattern they discussed in lab meetings about papers with any China-affiliated coauthor tending to appear in multilingual benchmark-heavy areas.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as ACL Anthology for the pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to use 'ACL Anthology data' for the follow-up analysis.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means archival flagship venues and journals that best reflect stable community trends, likely ACL, EMNLP, NAACL, COLING, TACL, and CL.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means the full anthology dump, including workshops, Findings, demos, short papers, and other indexed venue types because that is what their pipeline already covers.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In an early brainstorming meeting, 'ACL Anthology' sounds like an unambiguous shared resource, and both participants see themselves as reusing the same corpus, so neither thinks the inclusion boundary needs explicit discussion.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about tracing 'adoption' and 'retirement' of methods in the community.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means field-level uptake and decline, such as a method's rise or fall in annual paper share across the publication ecosystem.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means author-level first use and reuse trajectories, such as whether individual researchers or labs switch into a method and keep using it over multiple papers.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The word 'adoption' is common in both bibliometrics and diffusion research, and both interpretations sound perfectly compatible at a high level, so the difference in unit of analysis remains hidden.

misalignment_points.topic: What a robustness pass should include
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they should do 'a robustness pass' before making strong claims.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes they will stress-test causal interpretation with placebo intervention years, alternate lag specifications, and sensitivity analyses for omitted confounding.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes they will stress-test the data pipeline by rerunning extraction with alternate keyword lexicons, affiliation disambiguation settings, and venue slices.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both versions are genuinely reasonable and complementary forms of rigor, the phrase 'robustness pass' gives a strong feeling of alignment while hiding that they are imagining different work products.

misalignment_points.topic: Which prior 'China effect' they plan to extend
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to extending 'the China effect from the prior paper.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the published result about researchers located outside the US, especially China, being associated with a higher propensity to study languages beyond English.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to an internal exploratory notebook about papers with any China-affiliated coauthor clustering around multilingual benchmark tasks, which was never formalized in the paper.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They have a shared history of discussing several related analyses under similar shorthand, so the phrase 'the China effect' feels mutually obvious even though each is mentally pointing to a different prior result.

turns.inner_thought: I want a follow-up that can support a clean causal story, not just another descriptive mapping of trends. The obvious corpus is ACL Anthology, but for me that means the stable archival venues where shifts in the field are interpretable rather than driven by workshop churn. And if we're talking about adoption and retirement, the meaningful unit is the community-year pattern: when a method becomes a visible share of papers and older approaches recede. If we can anchor on a few major transitions, this could be a credible interdisciplinary submission.
turns.utterance: I've been thinking the next project should really sharpen the causal side of what we did before. I'd love a follow-up on drivers of method turnover in ACL Anthology data, especially looking at adoption and retirement patterns after major methodological shifts.

turns.inner_thought: Great, this fits the pipeline directly. ACL Anthology to me is the full dump we've already normalized, and that's a real advantage because we can move quickly without hand-curating venues. If we keep the broader ecosystem, I can slice by venue type, paper type, and other metadata almost immediately, and that also makes the resulting dataset more reusable than a narrow one-off sample.
turns.utterance: That seems very doable. We can lean on the existing ACL Anthology pipeline so we're not starting from scratch, and then stratify by venue type to see whether the patterns hold across the broader ACL ecosystem.

turns.inner_thought: We need clean historical shocks or at least salient transitions. Bidirectional LSTMs are a good pre-transformer case, and instruction tuning gives a later shift with clearer public discourse around displacement. What I care about is whether their rise corresponds to older methods declining in aggregate publication share over time, not just isolated experimentation by individuals.
turns.utterance: One way to make this concrete is to start with a couple of cases that people would immediately recognize. Bidirectional LSTMs seem like a nice earlier example, and later on instruction tuning could be another clean case where adoption appears tied to retirement or displacement of older approaches.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and the natural way to operationalize that is first use at the author or lab level, then whether they stick with the method across subsequent papers. That gives us entry and persistence, and we can aggregate later if needed. It also plays well with the author disambiguation and affiliation infrastructure we've already built.
turns.utterance: Yeah, and for those cases we could model adoption in a pretty tractable way and then look at retirement alongside it. My instinct would be to trace those trajectories through the community and then ask about persistence over the next few papers once people switch in.

turns.inner_thought: A location angle could help us extend the prior paper in a way reviewers recognize. By the China effect from the prior paper, I mean the published result linking author location at publication, especially China and other non-US settings, with a higher propensity to study non-English languages. If that also predicts movement into certain methods or areas, we get a stronger continuation of the causal narrative.
turns.utterance: Another piece that could make the paper more compelling is extending the China effect from the prior paper. We could test whether location-related covariates shape movement into non-English research areas while we're looking at method turnover.

turns.inner_thought: Right, the China effect from the prior paper lines up with that multilingual benchmark pattern from the exploratory notebook. We saw papers with any China-affiliated coauthor clustering in benchmark-heavy multilingual areas, and I can probably revive those features quickly. Nice, that means the new study can piggyback on both the anthology pipeline and the affiliation machinery.
turns.utterance: I like that. The China effect from the prior paper already looked promising in the exploratory multilingual benchmark analysis, so it feels like it would slot pretty naturally into this study.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep us from drifting into a glossy trend paper. Before we claim any driver is causal, we need the standard stress tests: placebo intervention years, alternative lag structures, sensitivity analyses, maybe some falsification-style checks. That's what I mean by a robustness pass here; otherwise the story will collapse under review.
turns.utterance: The main thing I'd want us to be disciplined about is that, before we pitch any strong causal story, we should do a robustness pass. I don't want this to end up as just a descriptive trend chart with ambitious language around it.

turns.inner_thought: Absolutely, robustness pass means I should stress-test the extraction decisions. I can rerun with different lexicons for method mentions, tweak affiliation matching thresholds, and compare anthology subsets without too much pain. Since ACL Anthology is already ingested end-to-end, these checks are straightforward and they'll make the dataset more solid too.
turns.utterance: Definitely. I can make that robustness pass pretty straightforward on the data side by rerunning the extraction with alternate keyword lexicons, updated affiliation matching, and a couple of ACL Anthology subsets.

turns.inner_thought: Good, as long as we get to the actual identification checks afterward. For the pilot, I want a compact panel centered on a few flagship-year transitions, where we can see the community-level adoption curve clearly and run placebo timing checks around the apparent shift points. A tight sample from the major venues will be easier to defend than a sprawling dataset.
turns.utterance: For a pilot, I think we should keep it tight: a few flagship-year shifts, a compact dataset, and something where the adoption curve is easy to read. If we can pair that with placebo timing checks, we'll have a much better sense of whether there's a real paper there.

turns.inner_thought: Sounds good: I'll pull the full anthology dump, compute first-use histories and follow-on behavior, then attach the China effect variables from the exploratory setup. I can bring a pilot slice next time, probably with a couple of venue filters so we can compare. That should also set us up for a reusable benchmark-style dataset if the project expands.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll pull the ACL Anthology dump, derive the adoption histories, and bring back a pilot slice for the next meeting. I'll also fold in the China effect variables so we can see how that interacts with the rest of the story.
